political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders. Scott’s studies of French feminists and the parity movement, known through her reviewers, examine claims to inclusion caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration

strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

black.label: Black history
black.description: Challenges racist historical narratives and recovers Black agency, institutions, and political struggle. Abolitionism, community scholarship, and Black institutions provide independent roots, not merely applications of European theory.

Woodson and colleagues founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (now ASALH) in 1915. Postwar and later examples include John Hope Franklin, From Slavery to Freedom (1947), and Darlene Clark Hine, Black Women in White (1989).

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
social.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). social.scope_note: Class formation, demographic reconstruction, communities, and everyday life have different methods; Marxist history is one substantial component. The 1950s–1970s label marks expansion, not termination: later mapped works extend and dispute these programmes. Earlier women’s social inquiry remains visible as comparison. Neither one European class trajectory nor transparent experience supplies a universal model; critical interventions do not erase productive inheritances.

strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987)

strands.title: Colonial labor and contested categories
strands.focus: Chakrabarty questions universal class narratives through Bengal jute workers; Cooper examines colonial labor classifications and African social relations. Neither supplies one model for all colonized workers.

strands.title: Experience, identities and historical explanation
strands.focus: Read Scott’s critique of foundational experience alongside Thompson’s historical class formation. Scott’s proposed historicization is not a consensus or a demand to abandon experience.
strands.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

strands.title: Peasant movements, belief and political aims
strands.focus: Hilton compares 1381 with continental movements while examining aims, allies and outcomes. Conflict does not mean constant open warfare; economic/social relations require political and religious analysis. Neither quick defeat nor later change settles causation.
strands.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973), selected introduction and conclusion

strands.title: Bandit narratives, political power and local research
strands.focus: Hobsbawm’s revised model responds to myth and patronage objections and draws on Colombian scholarship. Songs are mediated evidence; political actors and social settings cannot be inferred directly from heroic stories.
strands.works: Bandits (1969; revised edition 2000); Sánchez/Meertens (1987)

strands.title: Migration and the timing of observation
strands.focus: Ferrie’s response to Thernstrom asks who disappears from a local sample and what happens before its first observation. His male immigrant sample does not represent every worker or family.
strands.works: Ferrie (1996 manuscript),1–8,21

strands.title: Culture under capitalism: continuity or reworking?
strands.focus: Chakrabarty rejects deriving workers’ culture from economic function alone. Nair asks whether describing traditions as survivals makes them too fixed, and how their reworking within capitalism should enter the explanation.
strands.works: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989/2000), preface xi–xv; Nair review (1990), 98

strands.title: Separate spheres: categories, chronology and regional evidence
strands.focus: Davidoff and Hall connect class formation to gender and familial support. Vickery values their detailed research but questions its chronology and generalization: her Lancashire comparison crosses land and trade, while prescriptive language does not straightforwardly establish women’s confinement.
strands.works: Family Fortunes (1987), prologue opening; Vickery (1993), 393–401

strands.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
strands.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
strands.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

strands.title: Politics within social-history debate
strands.focus: Eley and Nield asked in 1980 why social history ignored politics (article unread; they recalled in 2007 that it 'drew disappointingly little response in print' and that they had been 'trying to create a space for political analysis in the expanded sense given to "politics" by the politics of knowledge of 1968', 2000, p. 14). Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). In 'Farewell to the Working Class?' (2000, read in full) they held that 'class discursively understood … is a better starting point' while wanting 'to break this logic of disavowal' (p. 16); Scott's reply (read in full) called this 'Assent to Discourse' and objected that insisting on class forecloses other political categories (p. 69); Cooper answered that 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980), coauthored; “Starting Over” (1995); “Farewell to the Working Class?” and reply (ILWCH 57, 2000); The Future of Class in History (2007)

nationalismstudies.label: Nationalism studies
nationalismstudies.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.
nationalismstudies.representative_figures_and_works: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (1983); Hobsbawm and Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); Anthony D. Smith; Partha Chatterjee, Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986).

nationalismstudies.scope_note: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm, Smith, and Chatterjee supply competing accounts, not a common modernist theory. Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.
